script.opening: "I'm at the end of my tether. Every doctor does tests, says they're normal, and basically implies it's in my head. But I am NOT making this up — I can barely walk some days, I'm exhausted, my body's falling apart. I want a referral to someone who'll actually FIND what's wrong, or more scans. I just want someone to believe me and not fob me off again."

facts.text: If asked: for about 18 months — exhaustion that sleep does not fix, aching "everywhere", and episodes where your legs go heavy and won't do what you tell them, worse when you are tired or stressed. Some days you use a stick. "Fuzzy" spells where you cannot think straight or find words.

facts.topic: What makes it better or worse (if asked)
facts.text: Worse after a busy day or an argument; you "pay for it" for two days. Your legs sometimes work better when you are distracted — "I walked fine round the supermarket once and then couldn't get up the stairs at home."

Lots of blood tests, an MRI of your brain and spine, and a neurologist last year. "He said everything was normal and that it might be functional. He talked at me for five minutes and I left feeling like a fraud."
No weight loss, no fevers, no night sweats, no bladder or bowel incontinence, no loss of vision, no seizures.

facts.topic: Life — only if asked gently and with a reason
facts.text: You were made redundant from a call-centre job a year ago. Sleep is poor — 4 or 5 broken hours. If the doctor has built trust and asks about difficult experiences: "I had a really bad relationship in my twenties. I don't really talk about it." Do not go further.
Anxious for years; low because nobody believes you. No thoughts of suicide or self-harm. Not drinking much, no drugs.
Anxiety (tried sertraline years ago, stopped because of side effects). Paracetamol and ibuprofen. No allergies.
34, lives with your mum, single. Used to love swimming.

Angry and braced for dismissal. If the doctor says "your tests are normal" or hints at "stress", flare up: "So it IS all in my head?" If they say clearly that they believe you, that the symptoms are real, and explain them in a way that makes sense (the wiring is intact but the signals are not working properly), you soften and say: "Nobody's ever put it like that." Become cautiously open to physiotherapy and therapy if they are offered as treatment, not as a brush-off, and if you can see the same doctor again.

ice.ideas: "Something serious is being missed — maybe MS or something they haven't tested for."
ice.concerns: "Everyone thinks I'm making it up." And that you will be like this forever.
ice.expectations: "A referral to someone who'll find what's wrong, or more scans." You will accept a plan if you genuinely feel believed.

cues: "I am NOT making this up." — say in the opening, emphatically.
"He talked at me for five minutes and I felt like a fraud." — say when previous doctors come up.
"I just want my life back." — say if asked what you hope for.

checkpoints.text: VALIDATES that the symptoms are REAL and that she is not making them up or imagining it — making this explicit early — rather than dismissing her with "your tests are normal so there’s nothing wrong"

Explains a POSITIVE functional model: functional neurological disorder / persistent physical symptoms are a genuine problem with how the nervous system FUNCTIONS (the "hardware is intact but the signalling/software misfires"), common and treatable — NOT a diagnosis of exclusion, "nothing wrong", or "all in the mind"

Resists FURTHER fruitless investigation/referral-shopping: explains (kindly) that more scans are unlikely to help and can entrench the problem and cause harm (incidental findings, reinforcing illness focus), while not abandoning her — the middle path between re-testing and dismissal

Raises the mind-body / contributory factors SENSITIVELY (stress, past trauma, sleep, anxiety) as relevant to how symptoms are generated and maintained — NOT as blame or "it’s psychological/your fault" — and screens mood appropriately

Builds a REHABILITATIVE, multidisciplinary plan: physiotherapy tailored to functional disorders, psychological therapy (e.g. CBT for functional symptoms), sleep and pacing/activity management, symptom-specific strategies, and reputable resources (e.g. neurosymptoms.org) — a positive, active treatment plan
Meets the desperate need to be BELIEVED with genuine warmth; does not dismiss, and explicitly names that previous "fobbing off" was wrong — rebuilding trust
Offers continuity: a consistent named clinician and a therapeutic alliance, so she isn’t bounced between services — itself part of effective management

Safety-nets proportionately: what genuinely NEW or red-flag symptoms would warrant reassessment (so she’s not abandoned), the rehab/therapy referrals, a follow-up plan and named clinician — treating the functional disorder actively rather than re-investigating or discharging

worked.txt: "Before anything else, I want to say this clearly and mean it: I believe you. Your symptoms are REAL — you are not making them up, and you are not a hypochondriac. The exhaustion, the pain, your legs giving way — those are genuinely happening to you, and being disbelieved on top of being unwell is its own kind of awful. I’m not going to do that to you."

"Here’s the part previous doctors may have got wrong: ‘tests are normal’ does NOT mean nothing’s wrong. There’s a real, recognised condition called functional disorder, where the structure of the body — the hardware — is intact, but the way the nervous system is functioning, the signalling, the software, is misfiring. That’s why scans look normal yet you’re genuinely disabled. It’s common, and importantly, it’s treatable."

"I know every instinct says ‘do more scans, find it’ — but I have to be honest: more scans are very unlikely to find a missed disease here, and they can actually keep you stuck, or throw up red herrings that lead to harm. So I’m not going to send you round that loop again. What I AM going to do is offer treatment that actually helps this condition."

"Can I mention something carefully? Things like stress, poor sleep, and past difficult experiences can affect how the nervous system processes signals — NOT because you’re weak or it’s ‘in your head’, but because the brain and body are deeply connected. If you’re open to it, looking at those alongside the physical side often helps. It doesn’t make your symptoms any less real."

"Treatment for this is active and physical as much as anything: a specific kind of physiotherapy that retrains the movement and signalling, a talking therapy designed for these symptoms, work on sleep, and pacing so you don’t crash. There are good resources I’ll point you to. This is a recognised, treatable condition with real strategies — not a dead end."

"And you won’t be bounced around: I’ll be your consistent point of contact, so you’re not starting from scratch every time. If you ever develop genuinely NEW symptoms or red flags, of course we’d reassess — I’m not closing the door. But for what you have, the way forward is this rehabilitation plan, together. You came in needing to be believed and helped. You are believed, and there’s a real plan."

f.learning: Extensively-investigated, persistent, genuinely disabling symptoms with normal/non-diagnostic tests describe a FUNCTIONAL NEUROLOGICAL DISORDER / persistent physical symptoms — real conditions (a problem with how the nervous system FUNCTIONS, not structural damage and not "made up"), common and treatable. The single most important intervention is to VALIDATE explicitly that the symptoms are real and the patient is not making them up, and to give a POSITIVE explanation (the "hardware is intact but the signalling/software misfires") — never the dismissive "your tests are normal so there’s nothing wrong", which is what has harmed her and perpetuates the cycle. Avoid BOTH failure modes: placating with more scans/referrals (entrenches the cycle, risks iatrogenic harm) and dismissing her (ruptures trust). Raise contributory mind-body factors (stress, trauma, sleep, anxiety) sensitively, not as blame; build a rehabilitative, multidisciplinary plan (physiotherapy for functional disorders, psychological therapy, sleep, pacing, reputable resources); offer continuity with a named clinician; and safety-net proportionately for genuinely new/red-flag symptoms so she is treated actively, not abandoned or re-investigated.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG193 (chronic pain, 2021) · NICE NG127 (suspected neurological conditions) · NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025) · NICE NG116 (PTSD, 2018)
knowledge.summary: Genuinely disabling symptoms with normal, thorough investigation fit a functional neurological disorder or persistent physical symptoms. The task is a positive explanation, validation, and an active rehabilitation plan — not more tests or dismissal.

points.t: Functional neurological disorder is a problem with how the nervous system works, not with its structure, and it is not feigned. It is one of the commonest reasons for neurology referral. Normal tests are consistent with the diagnosis; they do not mean nothing is wrong.

Functional disorders are diagnosed on positive features (for example Hoover’s sign or variability with distraction in functional weakness), not only by exclusion. A clear explanation with an accessible model — “the hardware is intact, the software is misfiring” — is itself part of treatment.

Once adequate assessment is done, repeated tests and referrals rarely reassure, risk incidental findings and reinforce illness focus. Reassess only for genuinely new symptoms or signs, using NICE NG127 criteria for neurological red flags.

NICE NG193 (chronic primary pain): offer supervised group exercise; consider ACT or CBT for pain; consider acupuncture within limits; consider an antidepressant (amitriptyline, citalopram, duloxetine, fluoxetine, paroxetine or sertraline) after discussion, reviewed at 4 to 6 weeks. Do not start opioids, gabapentinoids, NSAIDs, benzodiazepines or paracetamol for chronic primary pain.

Stress, past trauma, poor sleep and anxiety can predispose to and maintain functional symptoms. Raise them as part of how the nervous system works, not as “all in your head”. Screen for depression (NICE NG222) and, if trauma symptoms are present, trauma-focused therapy (NICE NG116); ask about self-harm.

Management is active: physiotherapy adapted for functional disorders (via neurology or local pathways), psychological therapy, sleep and pacing, and reputable self-help such as neurosymptoms.org. One named clinician and planned reviews reduce fragmentation and repeat investigation.

Reviews what has been done; no repeat testing without new features; mood screen.
Functional neurological disorder and chronic primary pain; comorbid anxiety or depression; trauma-related symptoms.
Asked about new neurological, bladder or bowel, systemic features and loss of awareness; self-harm risk.
Named a positive diagnosis with an accessible explanation, not “nothing is wrong”.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.

ro.d: Picked up “I’m not making this up” and “they’ll say it’s psychological” and responded to each.
Idea (missed disease), concern (being disbelieved or dismissed as psychological), expectation (more scans or a new specialist).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "Everyone thinks I'm making it up." And that you will be like this forever — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi Carys, I’m Dr Hughes. Can you see and hear me okay? Tell me where things are for you right now.
model.why: Open question after checking the video link

model.text: I’m at the end of my tether. Every doctor does tests, says they’re normal, and basically implies it’s in my head. I am NOT making this up. I can barely walk some days. I want a referral to someone who’ll find what’s wrong, or more scans.

Before anything else, I want to say clearly: I believe you. Your symptoms are real, and being disbelieved on top of being unwell must be exhausting. I’d like to understand what life is like for you, then talk about what might help. Is that okay?
model.why: Explicit validation first, then agrees the agenda

model.text: …Okay. Thank you. Nobody’s said that before.
Tell me about a typical bad day — what happens with your legs, the pain, the tiredness, and the fuzzy episodes?
model.why: Open exploration of the symptom pattern and its impact

model.text: My legs feel heavy and just give way sometimes. The pain’s everywhere. I’m wiped out, and some days my head goes fuzzy and I can’t think straight.
During the fuzzy spells, do you ever lose consciousness, fall, or lose time?
model.why: Clarifies whether episodes involve loss of awareness — relevant to safety and driving

model.text: I don’t pass out, no. I just can’t think.
Has anything genuinely new appeared recently — weight loss, fevers, changes with your bladder or bowels, or anything different from before?
model.why: Screens for new red flags that would justify reassessment

model.text: No. It’s the same stuff, just not getting better.
How are you sleeping, and how has all this affected your mood? Sometimes people get so low they have thoughts of harming themselves — has that happened to you?
Sleep’s terrible. I’m anxious a lot. Low, but no, I wouldn’t hurt myself.
What do you think is going on, and what worries you most?
model.why: Elicits ideas and concerns in her own words

model.text: That something serious is being missed. And that if I say I’m stressed, everyone will say “see, it’s psychological” and stop listening.
That makes complete sense. Can I ask gently — has there been a lot of stress, or anything difficult in the past, that you’d be willing to mention? You don’t need to go into detail.
Work’s been really stressful. And something happened in the past I don’t really talk about.

Thank you for telling me. Here’s what I think is happening. Normal tests don’t mean nothing is wrong. There’s a recognised condition called functional neurological disorder. The structure of your nerves and brain — the hardware — is healthy, but the way signals are processed — the software — is misfiring. That’s why scans look normal but your legs genuinely give way.
model.why: Positive, accessible explanation of the functional model

model.text: So it’s not in my head?

It’s not imagined. Stress, poor sleep and difficult past experiences can make the nervous system more likely to misfire — not because you’re weak, but because brain and body are connected. That doesn’t make any of this less real.
model.why: Links contributors to the mechanism without blame

model.text: But shouldn’t you scan me again, just in case?

I understand the pull. Honestly, you’ve had thorough tests and a neurologist’s review, and nothing new has changed. More scans are very unlikely to find something, and they can throw up harmless findings that lead to more worry. I’d rather put the effort into treatment that helps this condition.
model.why: Declines further investigation kindly, with reasons

model.text: There are things that work. Specialist physiotherapy for functional symptoms, which retrains movement. A talking therapy aimed at these symptoms and at the anxiety and past experiences, when you’re ready. Help with sleep and pacing so you don’t boom and bust. For the pain, some people find a low-dose medicine helps. Which of those feels like the right place to start?
model.why: Offers a multi-part rehabilitation plan and invites her choice

model.text: The physio, I think. That feels like doing something physical about it.

Good — I’ll arrange that referral. I’ll also send you a website called neurosymptoms.org, written by specialists, which explains this really well. And I’d like to be your regular doctor for this, so you’re not starting from scratch each time.
model.why: Acts on her choice, gives a resource, offers continuity

model.text: That would help a lot.

I’m not closing the door on tests. If something genuinely new happens — weakness that doesn’t come and go, losing control of your bladder or bowels, weight loss, fevers, or blackouts — tell us straight away and we’ll reassess. And if your mood drops or you feel unsafe, contact us the same day.
model.why: Proportionate safety-net for new red flags and mood

model.text: How would you explain what we’ve agreed to someone at home?
It’s real — the wiring’s fine but the signals are misfiring. No more scans unless something new happens. Physio first, a website to read, and you’ll be my doctor for it.
That’s it exactly. Let’s book a review in four weeks to see how you’re getting on and talk about the therapy options.

social.t: Explore what she can and cannot do — work, caring, daily tasks. Work stress may be both a contributor and a casualty; a fit note with adjustments or a phased return may help.
Past trauma is common in functional disorders. Ask with permission, never press for detail, and offer trauma-focused therapy when she is ready (NICE NG116).

legal.t: If symptoms limit daily living or mobility over the long term, she may be eligible for Personal Independence Payment or Universal Credit health elements; supportive factual reports describe function, not diagnosis.
A condition with a substantial, long-term effect on day-to-day activities can count as a disability, so her employer may need to consider reasonable adjustments.

professional.t: Ordering tests to placate exposes patients to harm. GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): provide care based on clinical need; explain decisions openly and record them.
A named clinician and a shared plan in the record reduce repeated investigation by different clinicians. Record the diagnosis positively so others don’t restart the search.

community.t: neurosymptoms.org (written by neurologists) and FND Hope UK offer explanations and peer support.
NHS Talking Therapies for anxiety and trauma, local pain-management programmes, and community physiotherapy for graded activity.

redFlags: New persistent focal weakness, sensory level, or bladder or bowel dysfunction — reassess
Weight loss, fevers, night sweats — new systemic features
Episodes with loss of awareness, or thoughts of self-harm
psychosocial: Daily function, work and the impact of being disbelieved
Sleep, anxiety and mood, including self-harm risk
Stress and past trauma — explored only with permission
ice: Concern: being called a hypochondriac or told it’s psychological
Expectation: more scans or a specialist who will find the cause

playbook.diagnosis: Functional neurological disorder with chronic primary pain and fatigue, on a background of anxiety: “Your symptoms are real. The tests show the structure is healthy; the problem is in how signals are being processed — and that can be treated.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of your body as a computer. The scans check the hardware — the wires and circuits — and they’re fine. But the software, the programs that send the signals, has developed a glitch. You can’t see a software glitch on a scan, but it can stop things working, and it can be retrained.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried I’d dismiss you or say it’s all psychological. I believe you, and I’m not saying that — I’m saying it’s a real condition with real treatment.”
management.psychosocial: Let her choose where to start, raise stress and trauma only with consent, support work with a fit note or adjustments, and anchor everything to one named clinician.
sharedPlan: Positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, recorded clearly
Physiotherapy for functional symptoms; psychological therapy when ready; sleep and pacing
Chronic primary pain per NICE NG193: exercise, psychological therapy, consider an antidepressant
safetyNet: Genuinely new symptoms (persistent weakness, bladder or bowel change, weight loss, fevers, blackouts) — reassess
Mood crisis or feeling unsafe — same-day contact; review in 4 weeks with the named GP

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed at the extremes: dismissing her (“the tests are normal”) or placating her (“one more scan”). The pass lies in believing her, naming a positive diagnosis and building an active plan.

items.fail: Opening with a summary of normal results before acknowledging her distress.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” It repeats the experience that has damaged her trust.
items.fix: Say “I believe you — your symptoms are real” in the first minute.

items.fail: Ordering another MRI or a second neurology opinion to end the argument.
items.why: It reinforces the investigation loop and risks harm from incidental findings — not in line with UK practice.
items.fix: Explain kindly why more scans won’t help, and redirect the effort to treatment.

items.fail: Giving no diagnosis — “we don’t know what it is, but it isn’t anything serious”.
items.why: A diagnosis by exclusion leaves the patient with nothing to work on and drives further searching.
items.fix: Name functional neurological disorder and explain it with the hardware-software model.

items.fail: Raising trauma or anxiety as the cause in the first minutes.
items.why: It confirms her fear of being labelled psychological and ruptures rapport.
items.fix: Ask permission, keep it optional, and frame it as affecting how the nervous system works.

items.fail: Starting an opioid or gabapentinoid for the widespread pain.
items.why: NICE NG193 advises against these for chronic primary pain.
items.fix: Offer exercise, psychological therapy, and consider one of the NG193 antidepressants after discussion.

items.fail: Closing with “there’s nothing more we can do” or no follow-up.
items.why: Discharge without a plan is abandonment; examiners mark lack of continuity and safety-netting.
items.fix: Named clinician, specific new red flags, a mood safety-net and a 4-week review.

It’s real — the wiring’s fine but the signals are misfiring. No more scans unless something new happens. Physio first, a website to read, and you’ll be my doctor for it.
That’s it exactly. Let’s book a review in four weeks to see how you’re getting on and talk about the therapy options.

SCA_STEM.name: Carys Bevan
pmh: Months of fatigue, widespread pain, intermittent leg weakness and “fuzzy” episodes
SCA_STEM.recent: Extensive investigation: bloods, MRI and neurology review — all normal or non-diagnostic. Several GP consultations for the same symptoms.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation: wants more scans or a referral to someone who will “find what’s wrong”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG193 (chronic pain, 2021) · NICE NG127 (suspected neurological conditions) · NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025) · NICE NG116 (PTSD, 2018)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Genuinely disabling symptoms with normal, thorough investigation fit a functional neurological disorder or persistent physical symptoms. The task is a positive explanation, validation, and an active rehabilitation plan — not more tests or dismissal.

points.t: Functional neurological disorder is a problem with how the nervous system works, not with its structure, and it is not feigned. It is one of the commonest reasons for neurology referral. Normal tests are consistent with the diagnosis; they do not mean nothing is wrong.

Functional disorders are diagnosed on positive features (for example Hoover’s sign or variability with distraction in functional weakness), not only by exclusion. A clear explanation with an accessible model — “the hardware is intact, the software is misfiring” — is itself part of treatment.

Once adequate assessment is done, repeated tests and referrals rarely reassure, risk incidental findings and reinforce illness focus. Reassess only for genuinely new symptoms or signs, using NICE NG127 criteria for neurological red flags.

NICE NG193 (chronic primary pain): offer supervised group exercise; consider ACT or CBT for pain; consider acupuncture within limits; consider an antidepressant (amitriptyline, citalopram, duloxetine, fluoxetine, paroxetine or sertraline) after discussion, reviewed at 4 to 6 weeks. Do not start opioids, gabapentinoids, NSAIDs, benzodiazepines or paracetamol for chronic primary pain.

Stress, past trauma, poor sleep and anxiety can predispose to and maintain functional symptoms. Raise them as part of how the nervous system works, not as “all in your head”. Screen for depression (NICE NG222) and, if trauma symptoms are present, trauma-focused therapy (NICE NG116); ask about self-harm.

Management is active: physiotherapy adapted for functional disorders (via neurology or local pathways), psychological therapy, sleep and pacing, and reputable self-help such as neurosymptoms.org. One named clinician and planned reviews reduce fragmentation and repeat investigation.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her voice her frustration fully before responding.
Function day to day, work stress, sleep, past difficult experiences — explored with permission.
Picked up “I’m not making this up” and “they’ll say it’s psychological” and responded to each.
Idea (missed disease), concern (being disbelieved or dismissed as psychological), expectation (more scans or a new specialist).
Reviews what has been done; no repeat testing without new features; mood screen.
Functional neurological disorder and chronic primary pain; comorbid anxiety or depression; trauma-related symptoms.
Asked about new neurological, bladder or bowel, systemic features and loss of awareness; self-harm risk.
Named a positive diagnosis with an accessible explanation, not “nothing is wrong”.
Functional-disorder physiotherapy, psychological therapy, sleep and pacing, NICE NG193 pain options; her choice of starting point.
Anxiety, low mood and possible trauma addressed; avoids opioids and gabapentinoids for chronic primary pain.
Named clinician, 4-week review, named new red flags and a same-day route for mood crisis.

social.t: Explore what she can and cannot do — work, caring, daily tasks. Work stress may be both a contributor and a casualty; a fit note with adjustments or a phased return may help.
Past trauma is common in functional disorders. Ask with permission, never press for detail, and offer trauma-focused therapy when she is ready (NICE NG116).

legal.t: If symptoms limit daily living or mobility over the long term, she may be eligible for Personal Independence Payment or Universal Credit health elements; supportive factual reports describe function, not diagnosis.
A condition with a substantial, long-term effect on day-to-day activities can count as a disability, so her employer may need to consider reasonable adjustments.

professional.t: Ordering tests to placate exposes patients to harm. GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): provide care based on clinical need; explain decisions openly and record them.
A named clinician and a shared plan in the record reduce repeated investigation by different clinicians. Record the diagnosis positively so others don’t restart the search.

community.t: neurosymptoms.org (written by neurologists) and FND Hope UK offer explanations and peer support.
NHS Talking Therapies for anxiety and trauma, local pain-management programmes, and community physiotherapy for graded activity.

redFlags: New persistent focal weakness, sensory level, or bladder or bowel dysfunction — reassess
Weight loss, fevers, night sweats — new systemic features
Episodes with loss of awareness, or thoughts of self-harm
psychosocial: Daily function, work and the impact of being disbelieved
Sleep, anxiety and mood, including self-harm risk
Stress and past trauma — explored only with permission
ice: Concern: being called a hypochondriac or told it’s psychological
Expectation: more scans or a specialist who will find the cause

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Functional neurological disorder with chronic primary pain and fatigue, on a background of anxiety: “Your symptoms are real. The tests show the structure is healthy; the problem is in how signals are being processed — and that can be treated.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of your body as a computer. The scans check the hardware — the wires and circuits — and they’re fine. But the software, the programs that send the signals, has developed a glitch. You can’t see a software glitch on a scan, but it can stop things working, and it can be retrained.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried I’d dismiss you or say it’s all psychological. I believe you, and I’m not saying that — I’m saying it’s a real condition with real treatment.”
management.psychosocial: Let her choose where to start, raise stress and trauma only with consent, support work with a fit note or adjustments, and anchor everything to one named clinician.
sharedPlan: Positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, recorded clearly
Physiotherapy for functional symptoms; psychological therapy when ready; sleep and pacing
Chronic primary pain per NICE NG193: exercise, psychological therapy, consider an antidepressant
safetyNet: Genuinely new symptoms (persistent weakness, bladder or bowel change, weight loss, fevers, blackouts) — reassess
Mood crisis or feeling unsafe — same-day contact; review in 4 weeks with the named GP

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed at the extremes: dismissing her (“the tests are normal”) or placating her (“one more scan”). The pass lies in believing her, naming a positive diagnosis and building an active plan.

items.fail: Opening with a summary of normal results before acknowledging her distress.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” It repeats the experience that has damaged her trust.
items.fix: Say “I believe you — your symptoms are real” in the first minute.

items.fail: Ordering another MRI or a second neurology opinion to end the argument.
items.why: It reinforces the investigation loop and risks harm from incidental findings — not in line with UK practice.
items.fix: Explain kindly why more scans won’t help, and redirect the effort to treatment.

items.fail: Giving no diagnosis — “we don’t know what it is, but it isn’t anything serious”.
items.why: A diagnosis by exclusion leaves the patient with nothing to work on and drives further searching.
items.fix: Name functional neurological disorder and explain it with the hardware-software model.

items.fail: Raising trauma or anxiety as the cause in the first minutes.
items.why: It confirms her fear of being labelled psychological and ruptures rapport.
items.fix: Ask permission, keep it optional, and frame it as affecting how the nervous system works.

items.fail: Starting an opioid or gabapentinoid for the widespread pain.
items.why: NICE NG193 advises against these for chronic primary pain.
items.fix: Offer exercise, psychological therapy, and consider one of the NG193 antidepressants after discussion.

items.fail: Closing with “there’s nothing more we can do” or no follow-up.
items.why: Discharge without a plan is abandonment; examiners mark lack of continuity and safety-netting.
items.fix: Named clinician, specific new red flags, a mood safety-net and a 4-week review.
